About

Seismology across scales

My research spans structural and environmental seismology. I use the phase, amplitude, and temporal evolution of seismic wavefields to investigate volcanic and sedimentary-basin structure, scattering at sharp boundaries, subsurface hydrology, and dynamic surface processes.

Across these topics, I combine dense observations with wavefield physics and numerical modeling to place quantitative constraints on Earth structure and processes that change through time.

Current research

Recent and ongoing research

My current research focuses on imaging magmatic structure beneath the Cascades and using long-term seismic observations to understand how seasonal environmental processes influence waterfall forcing and erosion.

R
Ongoing · Cascades Arc

Seismic imaging of magmatic systems beneath southern Washington

We are developing a 3-D shear-wave velocity model of the southern Washington Cascades by integrating regional networks, temporary broadband stations, and dense nodal arrays—including a new 240-node deployment near Mount Rainier—and applying ambient-noise interferometry and adjoint surface-wave tomography to resolve the connectivity and depth variation of magmatic low-velocity structures.

≈
First-author manuscript · Submitted

Seasonal ice breakup increases the seismically measured force of waterfalls

A decade of seismic observations, controlled-source calibration, and 3-D wave simulations show that waterfall force generally scales with river discharge, while seasonal ice breakup can temporarily intensify channel-boundary impacts and potentially enhance erosion in climates with seasonal freezing.

Research

Research areas

My work brings together dense seismic observations, wavefield physics, and numerical modeling across three closely related areas.

Environmental Seismology

I use continuous seismic records and time-lapse measurements to track hydrologic change and quantify dynamic environmental forcing, including groundwater and waterfall processes.

Seismic Imaging & Tomography

I combine dense-array surface-wave observations with inverse and adjoint methods to image sedimentary basins, volcanic systems, and crustal structure from local to regional scales.

Wavefield Scattering

I use numerical simulations and theoretical analysis of surface-wave scattering to distinguish measurement artifacts from structural signals and to develop new sensitivity to sharp subsurface contrasts.

Research highlights

Submitted manuscript
Environmental seismology · Submitted

Seismically measured waterfall forces

A decade of seismic observations, controlled-source calibration, and 3-D wave simulations show that waterfall force generally follows river discharge, while seasonal ice breakup can produce transient increases in channel-boundary impacts with implications for erosion.

Zeng, Schaible, Schmandt, Farrell, Lin, Tsai & Koper

Zeng, Lin & Tsai (2024)
Wave propagation · GJI 2024

Apparent anisotropy from wavefield scattering

Numerical simulations and mode-coupling theory show that direction-dependent Rayleigh-wave phase velocities near sharp structural boundaries can arise from interference with scattered waves rather than intrinsic anisotropy. A 2026 follow-up study carries this sensitivity into an adjoint-tomography framework, using triple-difference surface-wave traveltimes to sharpen sensitivity to lateral velocity contrasts and structural boundaries.

2024 study ↗2026 follow-up ↗
Zeng, Lin & Allam (2022)
Dense-array imaging · The Seismic Record 2022

3-D imaging of Salt Lake Valley

Rayleigh-wave phase velocity and ellipticity measured across a temporary nodal array are combined to construct a 3-D shallow shear-wave velocity model of Salt Lake Valley, resolving basin structure relevant to regional seismic-hazard studies.
